Sources and methods

How to read the atlas

The atlas brings together reports of border closures and restrictions between 21 October 2016 and 21 October 2026. It is a record of past events. It does not provide live information about whether a border is open.

What does the dataset cover?

The dataset describes restrictions at land borders and international river ferries. A record can cover one crossing, several crossings or a wider rule. It may include several stages as restrictions changed.

Routine overnight opening hours, individual visa refusals and checks that allow passage are excluded.

How should I read the map?

Colour shows the recorded reason for a restriction. Along a land border, a solid line means the sources describe a restriction across that border. A dotted line means only some crossings were affected, or the extent is unclear.

The lines locate the records; they do not trace every closed section. Read each record for the affected people, goods, routes and exceptions. Unmarked does not necessarily mean open.

What do the dates mean?

Observed closure means a source reports that passage was stopped or restricted. Policy in force gives the dates of a rule. Announced closure dates come from a planned schedule. Repeated closures describes a period with closures and possible openings.

A record can appear in a month without covering every day of it. When the evidence gives only individual dates, or dates are disputed, the map shows those dates without filling the gaps. A last report of closure is not treated as a reopening date. Missing end dates are not extended to the present.

Days are calculated from recorded calendar dates. Same-day closures have no whole-day total; overlapping periods should not be added together.

How are the reasons grouped?

The categories, labelled “coded rationale” in the records, summarise reasons given in the sources. More than one category can apply to a record. An official explanation is recorded as such; it may not explain every reason for a closure.

Grey means no category has been assigned. This can reflect missing evidence or a reason that does not fit the categories.

Coverage varies by place, time and available sources. The charts describe the records collected. They do not measure how often closures happen worldwide. The duration charts use only land-border records with sufficiently clear dates and reopening evidence.

How do I find and download records?

Search looks across all recorded dates. After searching, you can use Map view to select restrictions recorded in a month, closures beginning in that month, or all records.

Click a line or record for a summary, dates and source links. Read all records opens a wider reading view. Download CSV saves every record matching your filters in a spreadsheet. Save view saves an image of the map and its key.

How can I check the sources?

Each record links to its sources and explains any uncertainty. Later reviews can correct earlier findings. Earlier findings are retained in the review history.

Some sources were available in full; others only as extracts. Different websites can repeat the same original report, so the number of links is not a count of independent confirmations.

Related records can describe parts of the same event. Record totals should therefore not be read as a count of separate closure decisions.

Island borders during COVID-19

Selected pandemic border rules for Australia, New Zealand and the UK appear separately on the map as outlines. Leaving these cases unmarked would misleadingly suggest that their borders were accessible during the pandemic. Each record explains who was affected and the exceptions. These additions are excluded from Analysis.
